title: After My Exchange Placement at Warwick Medical School
paragraphs: 1. Introduction From April to July 2008, I was given the opportunity to go on an exchange placement at Warwick Medical School in the UK. The three months in the UK were a succession of fresh and joyful days. At the same time, they were possible only because of the support of my family and friends in Japan and, above all, the wonderful people I met there. With gratitude to them, I would like to leave a record of my journey here.

2. Overview of Warwick Medical School Warwick is a town in Warwickshire, in the west-central part of England in the UK. It is also a town famous for Warwick Castle, a tourist attraction that retains the look of the Middle Ages. Nearby are towns such as Coventry, known for its bombing in the Second World War, and Leamington Spa, with its churches and parks.

The University of Warwick, my host university, is located ten minutes by car from Coventry. The university has the Warwick Arts Centre, one of the leading centres in England, where one can enjoy films, concerts and theatre. As for medical care, two large hospitals, the University Hospital Coventry and Warwickshire and Warwick Hospital, support the healthcare of Coventry and Warwick.

3. Overview of the Placement I did my placement mainly at the University Hospital Coventry and Warwickshire (hereafter UHCW), which is a university hospital, at Myton Hospice, which provides palliative care, and at a GP surgery in a village called Guilsborough. The breakdown is as follows. [At UHCW]

・Endocrine Department ・CCU/ICU ・Infection Control Team ・Specialist outpatient clinics: hypertension, diabetes, thyroid ・PACES (OSCE preparation for resident doctors) ・Accident & Emergency Department ・Observation of surgical operations
[At Myton Hospice] ・Palliative Care
[At the GP surgery] ・GP (placement at a British family doctor's surgery)

In addition, I was fortunate to have the opportunity to visit Helen & Douglas House, a hospice for children, attend the International Conference for Paediatric Palliative Care, visit part of the children's hospital Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children, and interview a Japanese paediatrician.

4. Endocrine Department The endocrine department is where I was first assigned and where I got used to the way placements work at UHCW. In most cases the method was that on the ward a resident showed me the patient list, and after obtaining permission I took the history and did the physical examination. Basically both the residents and the patients readily gave permission.

The patients I was able to see in the endocrine department included the following: CREST syndrome, phaeochromocytoma, alcoholic cirrhosis, hepatic coma, diabetic ketoacidosis, AS (aortic stenosis), anorexia nervosa, acromegaly and post multiple cerebral infarction. In the UK, specialties are set up on the premise that a physician is well versed in General Internal Medicine and a surgeon in General Surgery, so even on an endocrine ward a patient with AS may be admitted.

After taking the history and doing the physical examination, I often discussed the case with the resident. I was asked various things, such as the meaning of the findings I had obtained, the mechanism, the differential diagnosis and the tests needed next. The scene of one student's placement that I observed was very impressive. With an OSCE exam close at hand, she was assigned a single patient. First, the student alone took the history and did the physical examination. After that, the resident, who had been watching nearby, did the same history and physical examination and pointed out where she could improve. After finishing taking the findings, the two went to a separate room with no patient. The presentation began. She had to state properly everything from the patient's name, age, chief complaint and history, to positive findings and negative findings. Hardly had she finished the presentation when questions flew from the resident. "What are the patient's problems?" "If you classify those problems on the basis of pathophysiology and mechanism, what do you get?" "What is the most likely condition?" "What differential diagnoses can be considered from there?" "How will you proceed with diagnosis and treatment from here, including tests?" The discussion heated up. It lasted more than 30 minutes. And finally the test results and the actual diagnosis were revealed, and the teaching came to an end. Counting from the start of the history taking, they probably taught for an hour. I also received similar teaching, and it was again intensive, one to one. I felt that an educational system truly exists in which the student logically explains the pathology on the basis of the history and physical examination, and the resident teaches what is lacking.

5. CCU/ICU In the CCU/ICU, I was given an exercise in acid-base balance, in which we considered the blood gas results of patients admitted to the ICU. For values whose units differ from those in Japan, we consulted British medical books and discussed them. Although the placement period was short, it was an intensive placement in which I was asked to explain how I interpreted the results.

6. Infection Control Team I did a placement in this department for two weeks. The role of the ICT is to follow infectious disease patients expected to be difficult to control and to respond to consultations on antibiotic use. Specifically, in the morning I worked on testing in the laboratory, and in the afternoon the main work was rounds of patients in the ICU/CCU and after thoracic surgery. The laboratory work was mainly general tests for infectious diseases, such as Gram staining and antibiotic susceptibility testing. The afternoon rounds began with a daily conference. Around 1 p.m., the senior doctors of the ICT gathered, reported on new ICU/CCU patients and on patients consulted by other departments, and discussed them. After that, the senior doctor on duty that day and a specialty trainee went on rounds as a pair. The number of patients exceeded 30. The content of the rounds was to check at the bedside every day the drugs used and their doses and routes of administration. I got the impression that they paid particular attention to vancomycin and gentamicin. They also sometimes discussed future plans with the ICU/CCU doctors. I was told that even in the UK there is a tendency to use broad-spectrum antibiotics a lot, which is why the ICT manages antibiotics carefully. Other parts of their job are awareness-raising activities within the hospital and joint conferences related to infectious diseases. In particular, the card they had produced, which stated the in-hospital guidelines for empirical treatment when the causative organism has not been identified, was carried by many doctors. Another memorable event was a joint conference held after a report that postoperative infections were frequent in the orthopaedic ward.

7. Specialist Outpatient Clinics In the UK, senior physicians in internal medicine practise with a specialty. For example, the specialist clinics of the professor in charge of me were hypertension and diabetes. Along with observing those, I was also allowed to observe the clinic of a senior doctor who specialised in the thyroid. In the hypertension clinic, patients with poorly controlled hypertension are often referred from GPs (family doctors). There, after taking the history and doing the physical examination, one orders investigations such as of the RAA system. Here I was also allowed many times to take the history and perform the physical examination in advance, present to the senior doctor, and then see the patient together. In presentations, one is required to cover everything, of course the patient's name, age and chief complaint, but also the medication history, allergy history and systems review. In the diabetes clinic, I mainly saw many patients with type 1 DM, especially in the age group (late teens) transitioning from paediatrics to internal medicine. Some patients had social problems such as going to university or a partner's pregnancy, and for such patients a conference with nurses and other doctors is held after the consultation. I felt the importance of dealing with medical and social problems at the same time. Most of the patients in the thyroid clinic had thyrotoxicosis (hyperthyroidism), but some were patients with recurrence after thyroidectomy. Each patient was seen for about 20 minutes, followed by a discussion with the students.

8. PACES (OSCE for Resident Doctors) Preparation The UK is a country with a long history of the OSCE, and besides the OSCE for students there is also an OSCE for resident doctors. Both are conducted with the cooperation of patients, so candidates have their abilities tested just as in a real examination. This time I heard that a mock examination of PACES, the OSCE for resident doctors, would be held in the hospital, and I accompanied a resident and observed the whole process. Even though it was a mock examination, the senior doctor scored the resident's examination skills with the cooperation of real patients. There were many sections, and the ones that left an impression were: diagnosis of diabetic neuropathy, diagnosis of diabetic retinopathy, diagnosis of scleroderma, diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis, diagnosis of MR, judging the sound of a prosthetic valve after aortic valve replacement, diagnosis of liver cirrhosis, diagnosis of asbestosis, follow-up of a patient after thyroidectomy, and medical interviews (explaining to the family whether to insert an NG tube, explaining to a patient worried about myocardial infarction, explaining the results of metastasis of breast cancer to a patient), as well as advice for the actual examination. As this was practice, it ended with feedback from the senior doctor, but I heard that in the real examination it is so strict that only one in ten candidates passes. This is because of the marking method that "if there is even the slightest inconsistency in the diagnosis or in the process, that section is basically scored zero." From this too, I could glimpse an aspect of British medicine, which places importance on the history and physical examination.

9. Accident & Emergency In the UK, the emergency department is broadly divided into Major Injury, Minor Injury and, for children, the paediatric emergency outpatient clinic, and in addition, patients who need inpatient management, such as those with massive overdoses, are first admitted to the emergency department's ward. Doctors and nurses are assigned to all of these areas. Major Injury takes in patients who require many staff, such as traffic trauma, multiple trauma and acute myocardial infarction. In Minor Injury, on the other hand, mild to moderate walk-in patients with hand injuries or joint pain often come. The paediatric emergency department is, as the name suggests, specialised in children, and mostly saw trauma. In the emergency ward, the senior doctor and the specialty trainee made rounds as a pair, and handled things following the senior doctor's instructions. That trauma is common in the emergency department is probably largely due to the British healthcare system, in which for symptoms other than trauma the patient first sees a GP. However, I heard that some patients dislike the waiting time to see a GP and come directly to the emergency department.

10. Observation of Surgical Operations I was fortunate to become friendly with a specialty trainee in surgery and was able to observe operations. The cases I observed were laparoscopic cholecystectomy and peritonitis originating from appendicitis. In surgery, the division of roles is clear: foundation doctors mainly handle ward duties, and specialty trainees in principle concentrate on operations and postoperative rounds. A shift-based work system is also established, with normal duty, on-call (duty from daytime until 8 p.m.) and night shift. For this reason, I was told that even in surgery overtime and the like do not occur. In addition, a conference is held every Friday. There, residents and senior doctors have lively discussions about the cases who died that week, and the senior doctors give lectures, so I felt that the educational system is well established.

11. Career Forum At the University of Warwick, a career forum for medical students and resident doctors is also held. Here I would like to explain an outline of the British system of medical education. First, medical school in the UK is generally five years. However, a graduate-entry medical school such as Warwick Medical School is four years. There are also some six-year medical schools. After graduating from medical school, one proceeds to a two-year initial training course called the Foundation Years. Here one rotates through various departments and hones general medical skills. After that comes training in each specialty field. This is called Speciality Training. It is divided into three Levels, but during Level 1 one must pass the specialty training progression examination in order to advance to Level 2. This examination includes a written test and clinical skills. After completing about eight years of Speciality Training and receiving a certain evaluation through case reports and so on, one can at last become a Consultant (senior doctor).

12. Palliative Care The UK is also known as the birthplace of the hospice movement. This time I did placements at Myton Hospice, near Leamington Spa, and at the Mary Anne Evans Hospice, next to George Eliot Hospital. There are somewhat different aspects of hospices between the UK and Japan.

First, their operation is basically based on donations. The ways of collecting donations are varied, from ordinary donations, to the revenue of hospice charity shops often seen in towns, to volunteers planning small challenges ("taking on skydiving," "long-distance walking" and the like) and receiving donations from supporters if the challenge succeeds. In addition, the main purpose of admission is respite care. This is a form in which a patient is admitted to the hospice temporarily, for up to about two weeks, in order to control a worsened condition or to give the family caregivers a rest. In the background is the British home care system of GPs, cancer specialist nurses and visiting nurses. At the hospice I visited, in addition to such admissions, day care was also provided. The biggest difference is that hospices are built within the community rather than inside hospitals. This seems to be one expression of British medicine being rooted in the community. On the other hand, features shared with Japan are that comprehensive care is provided by a Multi Disciplinary Team composed of doctors, nurses, social workers, chaplains and others, and the content of the care (methods of symptom control, methods of drug administration and so on). I would also add that palliative care doctors sometimes go to community hospitals and respond to consultations on symptom control.

13. GP Surgery One of the major characteristics of the British healthcare system is the existence of the GP, that is, the General Practitioner. The GP is a primary care specialist who handles a wide range of patients from infants to the elderly and a wide variety of conditions, from internal medicine to minor surgery, paediatrics and psychiatry. In the UK, in principle one cannot go to a community hospital without a GP's referral letter. For this reason, GPs receive specialist training and are required to have the ability to deal with any primary care disease. The place where I did my placement was the GP surgery (clinic) in a village called Guilsborough. Although called a clinic, it was like a base where doctors, nurses, pharmacists, public health nurses and others worked, and some of them did home visits. Starting with the doctors' consultations, they are in principle by appointment. Patients make an appointment by telephone or similar and then come in. There is also a rule that a GP must see a patient within 24 hours of the patient's request. The patients I observed included follow-up of DM and hypertension and rashes in infants. Among the nurses, the profession that interested me was the Nurse Practitioner. This is a nurse who has been given almost the same authority as a doctor. Specifically, the advantage is that they can see patients and prescribe drugs on their own. The things they cannot do are referral to other hospitals and ordering CT, MRI and the like. I would also note that in the UK postgraduate education for nurses is well developed, and specialist nurses, such as asthma specialists and heart failure specialists, are recognised and active. In addition, I was allowed to observe public health nurses' home visits to mothers and infants and antenatal check-ups. Seeing the attitude of listening carefully to patients even in ordinary consultations and the frequent home visits, I felt that I saw there the shape of "medicine that walks together with the community."

14. About Paediatric Palliative Care Paediatric palliative care, like that for adults, is a field that originated in the UK. It stems from the establishment in 1982 in Oxford of Helen House, a hospice for children. Later Douglas House, a hospice for young adults, was also established, leading to today's Helen & Douglas House. After the establishment of Helen House, children's hospices were set up around the UK, and I was told that there are now about 30. Like adult hospices, most are run on donations. The diseases that children's hospices target are
mostly central nervous system diseases such as adrenoleukodystrophy and cerebral palsy, and neuromuscular diseases such as muscular dystrophy,

and there are few neoplastic diseases. This is because, thanks to the presence of cancer specialist nurses, a system exists in which neoplastic diseases are seen at home. The current state of paediatric palliative care, represented by Helen & Douglas House, is worlds apart from that in Japan. Children can use these dream-like facilities free of charge, with their large gardens, jacuzzi, music room, computer room, play room, rooms for parents to rest in, and well-appointed mortuary.

The centres of paediatric palliative care at present are Cardiff University in Wales and Great Ormond Street Hospital in London. This time I took part in the 4th International Conference for Paediatric Palliative Care held at Cardiff University, and those three days were very interesting.

I was able to hear a wide range of presentations, from the current state of paediatric palliative care and its educational system to efforts for children with AIDS in Africa. It is worth noting that in the UK the ACT (Association for Children's Palliative Care) is working to establish paediatric palliative care, and that a movement has begun toward icpcn (the International Children's Palliative Care Network), which links paediatric palliative care in different countries.

15. Visit to Great Ormond Street Hospital Great Ormond Street Hospital, established in 1852, is the first children's hospital in the UK. This time I was allowed to visit this hospital's museum and the ground floor. The museum is small, but it preserves instruments and documents that tell the history of the hospital. The ground floor also has a large chapel.
Great Ormond Street Hospital is affiliated with the University of London and is also world-famous as a cutting-edge research centre.
16. Interview with a Japanese Paediatrician Fortunately, this time I was able to hear from a Japanese paediatrician working in Manchester (now moved to London).

The features of British paediatric care are that, in principle, only paediatricians see children, the presence of Play Therapists, and an attitude of respect for children and their parents. A Play Therapist is a kind of nursery nurse working on the ward, whose role is mainly to distract, through toys and so on, children who are frightened of procedures. Thanks to them, procedures often end without the child crying. In addition, a culture of respecting the child as an individual has taken root, and efforts are made to avoid as far as possible holding a child down, even as part of a procedure. At the same time, parents being present during procedures is recognised as a matter of course, and from the intravenous line to lumbar puncture, parents can stay by the child's side if they wish. Scenes like these were also practised in the paediatric emergency department of the university hospital where I did my placement. It may be a trivial matter, but I felt that each of these practices contributes to creating a society that respects children.

17. Interaction with Medical Students Interaction with local medical students was also very stimulating. Reuniting with medical student friends, taking part in a medical student party and talking with medical students with whom I newly formed friendships in Warwick are warm moments of memory.

18. Conclusion After finishing the three-month placement, I set out for home. If I were to describe these three months, I think they were "a time colored by encounters." Encounters with enthusiastic education, with community medicine, with a society that respects children, and above all with attractive doctors, nurses and medical students. In British healthcare, which has many challenges, the time I spent with them, who tackle medicine seriously, was irreplaceable.
I intend to take everything I learned and felt in the UK as nourishment and keep moving forward step by step.

Finally, I would like to close by expressing my great gratitude to everyone at the Nagoya University International Exchange Office and Academic Affairs Division who supported this exchange placement, to my classmates who went abroad with me, and to my family.
